# 1. Problem Description

The characteristics of cells collected from breast masses can provide useful information when comparing malignant and benign diagnoses. We investigate the following research question: **Can characteristics of breast masses quantify the differences between malignant and benign cases, and how accurately can we estimate the typical size associated with malignant cases?**

We use the Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer dataset, which contains measurements computed from digitized images of fine needle aspirates (FNA) of breast masses. These measurements describe the **cell nuclei**, not the dimensions of entire tumors. We therefore use mean nuclear area as our size variable and interpret our results accordingly. In particular, our principal population quantity of interest is the expected mean nuclear area for malignant observations. We also examine benign observations to provide a meaningful comparison.

# 2. Choice of Statistical Model

Mean nuclear area is strictly positive. We choose the **Gamma distribution**, a continuous distribution supported on positive values that can describe a right-skewed pattern. We fit one Gamma distribution to malignant observations and another to benign observations, since the two groups may differ in both center and spread.

Let $X_M$ and $X_B$ denote mean nuclear area for malignant and benign cases, respectively. Our working models are

$$
X_M\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(k_M,\beta_M),\qquad
X_B\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(k_B,\beta_B),
$$

where $k>0$ denotes shape and $\beta>0$ denotes **rate**. In this parameterization, the probability density function is

$$
f(x;k,\beta)=\frac{\beta^k}{\Gamma(k)}x^{k-1}e^{-\beta x},\quad x>0,
$$

and zero otherwise. The mean and variance are

$$
E(X)=\frac{k}{\beta},\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{k}{\beta^2}.
$$

Our central parameter of interest is $\mu_M=k_M/\beta_M$; the corresponding benign mean is $\mu_B=k_B/\beta_B$. These distributions are statistical approximations rather than statements that nuclear area follows a Gamma law exactly.

# 3. Dataset Description and Preparation

## 3.1. Dataset Description

The [Breast Cancer Wisconsin (Diagnostic) dataset](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/17/breast+cancer+wisconsin+diagnostic) contains measurements from digitized breast-mass FNA images. An observation represents one diagnostic case and is labeled **M** (malignant) or **B** (benign). The 30 numerical features summarize ten cell-nucleus characteristics, including area, radius, perimeter, texture, smoothness, and shape characteristics. We analyze `area_mean`: the **mean cell-nucleus area** associated with a case. The dataset documentation does not provide a physical unit for this feature, so we refer to **dataset units** rather than square millimeters.

The accompanying CSV is an export of the diagnostic dataset as distributed by scikit-learn. Its identification field is omitted, but all 569 observations and the 30 numerical measurements are retained.

## 3.2. Data Preparation

We import the CSV and check its dimensions, variable types, missing or nonfinite values, duplicate records, and positive area measurements. No missing values are imputed and no cases are removed.

```{r data-import}
# The CSV is kept in the project so this report works without web access.
if (!file.exists("data/wdbc_project.csv")) {
  stop("Could not find data/wdbc_project.csv. Open the RStudio project folder.")
}

bc <- read.csv("data/wdbc_project.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

stopifnot(
  nrow(bc) == 569,
  ncol(bc) == 31,
  all(c("diagnosis", "area_mean") %in% names(bc)),
  all(bc$diagnosis %in% c("M", "B"))
)

# Inspect the numerical variables and check the dataset structure.
numerical <- bc[, names(bc) != "diagnosis", drop = FALSE]
stopifnot(all(vapply(numerical, is.numeric, logical(1))))

missing_count <- sum(is.na(bc))
nonfinite_count <- sum(!is.finite(as.matrix(numerical)))
duplicate_count <- sum(duplicated(bc))
nonpositive_count <- sum(bc$area_mean <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)

if (missing_count > 0 || nonfinite_count > 0 || nonpositive_count > 0) {
  stop("Check data quality and positive Gamma support before analysis.")
}

x_M <- bc$area_mean[bc$diagnosis == "M"]
x_B <- bc$area_mean[bc$diagnosis == "B"]
```

There are `r nrow(bc)` observations, of which `r length(x_M)` are malignant and `r length(x_B)` are benign. The dataset has `r missing_count` missing entries, `r nonfinite_count` nonfinite numerical entries, `r duplicate_count` duplicate complete rows, and `r nonpositive_count` nonpositive mean nuclear-area measurements. No values were changed or excluded.

For modeling, we treat observations **within each diagnosis group** as independent and identically distributed. This is a working assumption, not a property that can be established from the CSV alone. Since these are clinical cases rather than a documented random sample of the population of all breast masses, results should not be generalized without caution.

## 3.3. Descriptive Statistics

We summarize the mean nuclear area within the two diagnosis groups. For the descriptive outlier check, we use R's default 25% and 75% sample quantiles to form an interquartile range. These are conventional interpolated quantiles; they need not equal the order-statistic quantiles used in our later Q-Q plots.

```{r descriptive-statistics}
# Here quantile() uses R's usual interpolated quartiles for the IQR
# descriptive outlier screening; the Q-Q plot below instead uses
# the order-statistic sample quantiles defined in CS108.
count_iqr_outliers <- function(x) {
  q <- as.numeric(quantile(x, c(0.25, 0.75)))
  iqr <- q[2] - q[1]
  sum(x < q[1] - 1.5 * iqr | x > q[2] + 1.5 * iqr)
}

area_summary <- data.frame(
  Diagnosis = c("Malignant", "Benign"),
  N = c(length(x_M), length(x_B)),
  Mean = c(mean(x_M), mean(x_B)),
  Median = c(median(x_M), median(x_B)),
  SD = c(sd(x_M), sd(x_B)),
  Minimum = c(min(x_M), min(x_B)),
  Maximum = c(max(x_M), max(x_B)),
  IQR_Outliers = c(count_iqr_outliers(x_M), count_iqr_outliers(x_B))
)

knitr::kable(
  area_summary,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Table 1. Summary of mean nuclear area by diagnosis"
)
```

The mean nuclear area is `r round(mean(x_M),2)` in the malignant group, compared with `r round(mean(x_B),2)` in the benign group: a ratio of approximately `r round(mean(x_M)/mean(x_B),2)`. The malignant group is also more variable (sample standard deviations `r round(sd(x_M),2)` versus `r round(sd(x_B),2)`).

```{r comparative-boxplot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="Figure 1. Mean nuclear area by diagnosis."}
boxplot(
  x_B, x_M,
  names = c("Benign", "Malignant"),
  col = c("lightblue", "lightpink"),
  main = "Mean Nuclear Area by Diagnosis",
  ylab = "Mean nuclear area (dataset units)"
)
```

The boxplots show generally larger nuclear-area values for malignant observations, while also showing overlap between the two groups. The conventional quantile-based $1.5\times IQR$ rule identifies `r count_iqr_outliers(x_M)` unusual values in the malignant group and `r count_iqr_outliers(x_B)` in the benign group. These values were retained: an extreme measurement is not necessarily an error, and removing it would change the tails of the observed distribution.

# 4. Relevance of the Gamma Model to the Data

We examine whether a Gamma model can reasonably describe the distributions of mean nuclear area **within each diagnosis group**. We compare observed values with a fitted density histogram, a Q-Q plot against theoretical Gamma quantiles, and the empirical versus fitted cumulative distribution functions.

## 4.1. Gamma Parameter Estimation by the Method of Moments

The Gamma models have two unknown parameters, so we match the **first and second theoretical moments** to the corresponding empirical moments, following the two-parameter Method of Moments.

Write

$$
m_1=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i,\qquad
m_2=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i^2.
$$

For $X\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(k,\beta)$, we have

$$
E(X)=\frac{k}{\beta},\qquad
E(X^2)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+[E(X)]^2
=\frac{k(k+1)}{\beta^2}.
$$

Thus the moment equations are

$$
\frac{k}{\beta}=m_1,\qquad
\frac{k(k+1)}{\beta^2}=m_2.
$$

Solving gives

$$
\boxed{\hat{k}=\frac{m_1^2}{m_2-m_1^2}},\qquad
\boxed{\hat{\beta}=\frac{m_1}{m_2-m_1^2}}.
$$

Here, $m_2-m_1^2=n^{-1}\sum_i(x_i-\bar{x})^2$ is the empirical variance with **denominator $n$**, not R's `var(x)`, which divides by $n-1$. We implement these formulas directly, without numerical root-finding.

```{r gamma-method-of-moments}
# Two-parameter Gamma Method of Moments using E(X) and E(X^2).
# These are raw empirical moments, so the implied variance has
# denominator n, not n - 1.
fit_gamma_mom <- function(x) {
  m1 <- mean(x)
  m2 <- mean(x^2)
  v <- m2 - m1^2

  if (v <= 0) stop("Gamma fitting requires positive empirical variance.")

  list(
    shape = m1^2 / v,
    rate = m1 / v
  )
}

fit_M <- fit_gamma_mom(x_M)
fit_B <- fit_gamma_mom(x_B)

fits_table <- data.frame(
  Diagnosis = c("Malignant", "Benign"),
  Shape = c(fit_M$shape, fit_B$shape),
  Rate = c(fit_M$rate, fit_B$rate),
  Fitted_Mean = c(fit_M$shape / fit_M$rate,
                  fit_B$shape / fit_B$rate)
)

knitr::kable(
  fits_table,
  digits = 6,
  caption = "Table 2. Method-of-Moments Gamma estimates"
)
```

The estimated shape and rate parameters are `r round(fit_M$shape,4)` and `r round(fit_M$rate,6)` for malignant observations, and `r round(fit_B$shape,4)` and `r round(fit_B$rate,6)` for benign observations. As expected from the first moment equation, the fitted Gamma means equal the sample means. Matching the mean does not itself establish a good distributional fit, so we examine the shape of the data next.

## 4.2. Density Histograms and Fitted Gamma Curves

A density histogram has total area one, so it can be compared with a probability density function. We use `hist(..., freq=FALSE, right=FALSE)` with R's default class intervals and overlay the Gamma densities calculated with `dgamma()`. The R commands are displayed alongside the resulting graphs so the analysis can be reproduced directly from this document.

```{r gamma-histograms, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.3, fig.cap="Figure 2. Density histograms with fitted Gamma curves."}
plot_hist_gamma <- function(x, fit, label) {
  grid_x <- seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = 400)
  gamma_y <- dgamma(grid_x, shape = fit$shape, rate = fit$rate)
  # Use R's default histogram intervals; plot=FALSE computes
  # density heights for setting a y-axis that also fits the curve.
  h <- hist(x, freq = FALSE,
            right = FALSE, plot = FALSE)

  hist(x, breaks = h$breaks, freq = FALSE, right = FALSE,
       col = "grey85", border = "white",
       ylim = c(0, 1.1 * max(c(h$density, gamma_y))),
       main = label, xlab = "Mean nuclear area", ylab = "Density")
  lines(grid_x, gamma_y, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot_hist_gamma(x_M, fit_M, "Malignant")
plot_hist_gamma(x_B, fit_B, "Benign")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The malignant measurements are spread over a wider range and have a longer right tail than the benign measurements. Both fitted curves capture the main concentration of observations, although deviations are visible, particularly in the tails of the malignant distribution. The histogram suggests that Gamma is a plausible approximation, not an exact description.

## 4.3. Theoretical Gamma Q-Q Plots

The Q-Q plot compares sample quantiles with theoretical Gamma quantiles. Following our course's definition, for ordered observations $x_{(1)}\leq\cdots\leq x_{(n)}$, the sample quantile at level $\alpha$ is

$$
q_\alpha^x=x_{(\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor)},
$$

with $x_{(0)}=x_{(1)}$ if the index is zero. We use the quantile levels $\alpha=0.05,0.10,\ldots,0.95$ and plot the pairs $(q_\alpha^F,q_\alpha^x)$, where $q_\alpha^F$ is calculated from the **fitted Gamma** distribution using `qgamma()`.

If the model fits the data, the points should be close to the bisector $y=x$.

```{r gamma-qq, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.3, fig.cap="Figure 3. Gamma Q-Q plots using the course's sample-quantile definition."}
# Lecture 06-07: q_alpha = x_(floor(alpha * n)); take x_(1)
# when floor(alpha * n) is 0.
course_sample_quantiles <- function(x, alpha) {
  ordered <- sort(x)
  indices <- pmax(1, floor(alpha * length(ordered)))
  ordered[indices]
}

plot_gamma_qq <- function(x, fit, label) {
  alpha <- seq(0.05, 0.95, by = 0.05)
  sample_q <- course_sample_quantiles(x, alpha)
  theoretical_q <- qgamma(alpha, shape = fit$shape,
                          rate = fit$rate)
  limits <- range(c(sample_q, theoretical_q))

  plot(theoretical_q, sample_q,
       xlim = limits, ylim = limits, asp = 1,
       pch = 19, cex = 0.8, col = "blue",
       main = label,
       xlab = "Theoretical Gamma quantiles",
       ylab = "Sample quantiles")
  abline(0, 1, col = "red", lwd = 2)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot_gamma_qq(x_M, fit_M, "Malignant")
plot_gamma_qq(x_B, fit_B, "Benign")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

For both diagnoses, the central quantiles are reasonably close to the reference line. Some deviations occur toward the larger quantiles, with more noticeable departures for malignant measurements. Because we compare only quantiles from 5% through 95%, these graphs do not directly include the most extreme 5% of observations in either tail.

## 4.4. Empirical and Fitted Cumulative Distributions

The empirical cumulative distribution function is

$$
F_n(t)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}I(x_i\leq t),
$$

where $I(x_i\leq t)$ equals one when an observation is at most $t$ and zero otherwise. It gives the observed proportion of measurements at or below a threshold. We compare this step function, calculated by `ecdf()`, with the fitted Gamma CDF calculated by `pgamma()`.

```{r gamma-cdf, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.3, fig.cap="Figure 4. Empirical and fitted Gamma cumulative distributions."}
# The empirical CDF compares observed cumulative proportions with
# probabilities calculated from the fitted Gamma distribution.
plot_gamma_cdf <- function(x, fit, label) {
  plot(ecdf(x), verticals = TRUE, do.points = FALSE,
       col = "grey40", main = label,
       xlab = "Mean nuclear area", ylab = "Cumulative probability")

  grid_x <- seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = 400)
  lines(grid_x,
        pgamma(grid_x, shape = fit$shape, rate = fit$rate),
        col = "blue", lwd = 2)
  legend("bottomright", c("Empirical CDF", "Fitted Gamma CDF"),
         col = c("grey40", "blue"), lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot_gamma_cdf(x_M, fit_M, "Malignant")
plot_gamma_cdf(x_B, fit_B, "Benign")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The empirical and fitted cumulative distributions are relatively close over much of the measurement range. Their differences are consistent with the imperfect alignment seen in the Q-Q plots. The Gamma model describes cumulative proportions reasonably well without matching every observed threshold exactly.

## 4.5. Assessment of Model Suitability

The three graphical comparisons indicate that separate Gamma distributions provide **reasonable approximations** to the observed mean nuclear-area distributions in malignant and benign cases. The model captures much of each group's center and overall shape, but discrepancies remain, particularly among larger malignant measurements. This makes caution especially important when interpreting very high quantiles or exceptionally large nuclear areas.

The substantial differences between malignant and benign measurements support analyzing the groups separately. Their combination need not follow a single Gamma distribution even if each group is approximately Gamma distributed.

These results do not establish that the distributions are exactly Gamma, nor do they establish random sampling or clinical representativeness. The analysis describes **mean cell-nucleus area in FNA observations**, not the physical size of an entire tumor.



# 6. Confidence Intervals by Elina

This section constructs and evaluates 95% confidence intervals for the population mean of `area_mean` among observations classified as malignant (`M`) in the Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer dataset.

The variable `area_mean` is positive and continuous. We use the Gamma model with shape parameter \(k\) and rate parameter \(\beta\). The parameter of interest is the population mean

\[
\mu = \frac{k}{\beta}.
\]

For a Gamma distribution parameterized by shape and rate,

\[
E(X)=\frac{k}{\beta},
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{k}{\beta^2}.
\]

The confidence intervals below are asymptotic intervals for \(\mu\). The Gamma parameter estimates are calculated only because they are needed to construct and simulate the confidence intervals.

## 6.1 Construction of confidence intervals

### Prepare the sample and estimate the Gamma parameters

The dataset was already imported in Section 3 from `data/wdbc_project.csv`.

```{r ci-data-preparation}
set.seed(108)

wdbc <- bc

# Keep malignant observations and select area_mean
malignant <- wdbc[wdbc$diagnosis == "M", ]
x <- malignant$area_mean

# Validate the sample (Section 3.2 found no missing or nonpositive values,
# so nothing is filtered; the check stops the analysis if this ever fails)
stopifnot(all(!is.na(x)), all(x > 0))

n <- length(x)
sample_mean <- mean(x)

cat("Number of malignant observations:", n, "\n")
cat("Sample mean:", sample_mean, "\n")
```

For a Gamma distribution with shape \(k\) and rate \(\beta\), the maximum likelihood estimates satisfy

\[
\widehat{\beta}=\frac{\widehat{k}}{\bar X},
\]

where \(\widehat{k}\) is obtained by solving

\[
\log(k)-\psi(k)
=
\log(\bar X)-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log(X_i).
\]

Here, \(\psi\) is the digamma function. We solve this equation numerically using `uniroot()`.

**Method of Moments versus MLE.** Section 4 used the Method of Moments (MoM) only to draw the fitted Gamma curves when checking the model. For the confidence intervals we use the **maximum likelihood estimates (MLEs)** of \(k\) and \(\beta\), because the standard error formula below comes from the asymptotic normality of the MLE and the Fisher information. The MoM and MLE parameter values therefore differ (for example, the malignant shape is about 7.10 by MoM and about 7.65 by MLE), but both give the same estimate of the mean, \(\widehat{\mu}=\bar X\).

```{r gamma-estimates}
gamma_mle <- function(values) {
  values <- values[!is.na(values) & values > 0]

  x_bar <- mean(values)
  s <- log(x_bar) - mean(log(values))

  equation <- function(shape) {
    log(shape) - digamma(shape) - s
  }

  shape_hat <- uniroot(
    equation,
    interval = c(0.000001, 1000000)
  )$root

  rate_hat <- shape_hat / x_bar

  c(
    shape = shape_hat,
    rate = rate_hat,
    mean = shape_hat / rate_hat
  )
}

estimates <- gamma_mle(x)

k_hat <- unname(estimates["shape"])
beta_hat <- unname(estimates["rate"])
mu_hat <- unname(estimates["mean"])

data.frame(
  Parameter = c("Shape (k)", "Rate (beta)", "Mean (mu)"),
  Estimate = c(k_hat, beta_hat, mu_hat)
)
```

Using the asymptotic distribution of the MLE and the Fisher information, the standard error of the mean estimator is μ/√(nk). Since μ and k are unknown, we estimate the standard error by plugging the MLEs μ̂ and k̂ into this asymptotic variance formula:

SE-hat(μ̂) = μ̂ / √(n k̂)
### Method 1: Normal (Wald) confidence interval

The Wald interval uses the asymptotic normal approximation:

\[
\widehat{\mu}
\pm
z_{0.975}SE(\widehat{\mu}).
\]

For a 95% confidence interval, \(z_{0.975}\) is approximately 1.96.

### Method 2: Log-transformed confidence interval

Since the population mean is positive, we can construct an interval on the logarithmic scale and then transform its endpoints back to the original scale:

\[
\left[
\exp\left(\log(\widehat{\mu})-
\frac{z_{0.975}}{\sqrt{n\widehat{k}}}\right),
\;
\exp\left(\log(\widehat{\mu})+
\frac{z_{0.975}}{\sqrt{n\widehat{k}}}\right)
\right].
\]

This interval is always positive and is generally asymmetric around the estimated mean.

### Calculate and compare the confidence intervals

```{r confidence-intervals}
confidence_level <- 0.95
alpha_level <- 1 - confidence_level
z_value <- qnorm(1 - alpha_level / 2)

se_mu <- mu_hat / sqrt(n * k_hat)

# Method 1: Wald normal confidence interval
wald_lower <- mu_hat - z_value * se_mu
wald_upper <- mu_hat + z_value * se_mu

# Method 2: Log-transformed confidence interval
log_se <- 1 / sqrt(n * k_hat)
log_lower <- exp(log(mu_hat) - z_value * log_se)
log_upper <- exp(log(mu_hat) + z_value * log_se)

ci_results <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Wald normal", "Log-transformed"),
  Estimate = c(mu_hat, mu_hat),
  Standard_Error = c(se_mu, se_mu),
  Lower = c(wald_lower, log_lower),
  Upper = c(wald_upper, log_upper),
  Length = c(
    wald_upper - wald_lower,
    log_upper - log_lower
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  ci_results,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "95% confidence intervals for the population mean"
)
```

The table reports the point estimate \(\widehat{\mu}\), its plug-in standard error (the same for both methods; the log-transformed interval applies the delta-method standard error \(1/\sqrt{n\widehat{k}}\) on the logarithmic scale), the lower and upper endpoints, and the length of each interval. The interval length measures its width: a shorter interval is more precise when its coverage is close to the nominal confidence level.

The confidence level describes the long-run performance of the interval procedure. If we repeatedly took samples and constructed intervals in the same way, approximately 95% of those intervals would contain the true population mean, assuming the model and approximation are appropriate. It is not correct to say that the fixed population mean has a 95% probability of belonging to this particular calculated interval.

## 6.2 Simulation study of the coverage probability

We use a simulation study to examine whether the two confidence interval methods achieve coverage close to the nominal 95% level.

We take the MLE estimates k̂ and β̂ from the malignant observations and treat them as fixed “true” parameter values for simulation purposes only; they are estimates, not genuinely known population parameters. The coverage results therefore describe how the methods behave when the data really come from a Gamma distribution with these parameters. For each simulated sample, we re-estimate the Gamma parameters and construct both confidence intervals. We record whether each interval contains the fixed true mean and calculate its length.

We use 5,000 repetitions for each sample size. The sample sizes include a smaller sample, the actual malignant sample size, and a larger sample.

```{r simulation-setup}
B <- 5000

# Treat the estimates from the real data as fixed true parameters
true_shape <- k_hat
true_rate <- beta_hat
true_mean <- true_shape / true_rate

sample_sizes <- sort(unique(c(30, n, 500)))

cat("Fixed true shape:", true_shape, "\n")
cat("Fixed true rate:", true_rate, "\n")
cat("Fixed true mean:", true_mean, "\n")
cat("Simulation repetitions:", B, "\n")
cat("Sample sizes:", sample_sizes, "\n")
```

### Run the coverage simulation

```{r coverage-simulation}
simulation_results <- data.frame(
  SampleSize = integer(),
  Method = character(),
  Coverage = numeric(),
  AverageLength = numeric()
)

for (sample_size in sample_sizes) {

  wald_covered <- logical(B)
  log_covered <- logical(B)

  wald_lengths <- numeric(B)
  log_lengths <- numeric(B)

  for (i in seq_len(B)) {

    # Generate a sample from the fixed Gamma model
    simulated_sample <- rgamma(
      sample_size,
      shape = true_shape,
      rate = true_rate
    )

    # Estimate the Gamma parameters from the simulated sample
    simulated_estimates <- gamma_mle(simulated_sample)

    simulated_shape <- unname(simulated_estimates["shape"])
    simulated_mean <- unname(simulated_estimates["mean"])

    # Estimated standard error for the sample mean
    simulated_se <- simulated_mean /
      sqrt(sample_size * simulated_shape)

    # Method 1: Wald interval
    wald_low <- simulated_mean - z_value * simulated_se
    wald_up <- simulated_mean + z_value * simulated_se

    # Method 2: Log-transformed interval
    simulated_log_se <- 1 /
      sqrt(sample_size * simulated_shape)

    log_low <- exp(
      log(simulated_mean) - z_value * simulated_log_se
    )
    log_up <- exp(
      log(simulated_mean) + z_value * simulated_log_se
    )

    # Record whether each interval contains the fixed true mean
    wald_covered[i] <- (
      wald_low <= true_mean && true_mean <= wald_up
    )

    log_covered[i] <- (
      log_low <= true_mean && true_mean <= log_up
    )

    # Record interval lengths
    wald_lengths[i] <- wald_up - wald_low
    log_lengths[i] <- log_up - log_low
  }

  simulation_results <- rbind(
    simulation_results,
    data.frame(
      SampleSize = sample_size,
      Method = "Wald normal",
      Coverage = mean(wald_covered),
      AverageLength = mean(wald_lengths)
    ),
    data.frame(
      SampleSize = sample_size,
      Method = "Log-transformed",
      Coverage = mean(log_covered),
      AverageLength = mean(log_lengths)
    )
  )
}

knitr::kable(
  simulation_results,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Empirical coverage and average interval length from 5,000 simulations"
)
```
simulation_wide <- reshape(
  simulation_results,
  idvar = "SampleSize", timevar = "Method", direction = "wide"
)
print(simulation_wide, digits = 5, row.names = FALSE)

write.csv(simulation_results, "simulation_results.csv", row.names = FALSE)

The empirical coverage probability is calculated as

\[
\widehat{p}
=
\frac{\text{Number of simulated intervals containing the true mean}}{B}.
\]

The average interval length is the mean of the lengths of the 5,000 intervals for each method and sample size.

### Compare empirical coverage with the nominal 95% level

```{r coverage-plot}
plot(
  simulation_results$SampleSize[
    simulation_results$Method == "Wald normal"
  ],
  simulation_results$Coverage[
    simulation_results$Method == "Wald normal"
  ],
  type = "b",
  pch = 16,
  ylim = range(c(0, 1, simulation_results$Coverage)),
  xlab = "Sample size",
  ylab = "Empirical coverage probability",
  main = "Coverage probability of the two confidence interval methods"
)

lines(
  simulation_results$SampleSize[
    simulation_results$Method == "Log-transformed"
  ],
  simulation_results$Coverage[
    simulation_results$Method == "Log-transformed"
  ],
  type = "b",
  pch = 17
)

abline(h = 0.95, lty = 2)

legend(
  "bottomright",
  legend = c("Wald normal", "Log-transformed", "Target: 95%"),
  lty = c(1, 1, 2),
  pch = c(16, 17, NA)
)
```

The horizontal dashed line represents the target coverage probability of 0.95. Values closer to this line indicate empirical coverage closer to the nominal 95% level.

### Compare average interval lengths

```{r interval-length-plot}
plot(
  simulation_results$SampleSize[
    simulation_results$Method == "Wald normal"
  ],
  simulation_results$AverageLength[
    simulation_results$Method == "Wald normal"
  ],
  type = "b",
  pch = 16,
  xlab = "Sample size",
  ylab = "Average interval length",
  main = "Average length of the confidence intervals"
)

lines(
  simulation_results$SampleSize[
    simulation_results$Method == "Log-transformed"
  ],
  simulation_results$AverageLength[
    simulation_results$Method == "Log-transformed"
  ],
  type = "b",
  pch = 17
)

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c("Wald normal", "Log-transformed"),
  lty = c(1, 1),
  pch = c(16, 17)
)
```

Shorter intervals indicate greater precision, provided that the coverage probability remains close to 0.95.
